14.meaning: what is correct / right — speech that is true, sound, and on the mark; the opposite of error or falsehood.
14.grammar: A noun in the accusative with the '-an' ending (tanwīn, the doubled 'n' sound 'an'). It is the object of 'said' — 'and says what is correct' — marking the content of the permitted speech.
14.root: ص-و-ب (ṣ-w-b) — to be right/correct, to hit the mark.

1.meaning: that — a demonstrative pointing to something distant or weighty: 'that (Day),' singling out the Day of Judgement just described.
1.grammar: A demonstrative pronoun meaning 'that (one, far off).' It is built from a core 'dhā' (that) plus the '-ka' element that addresses the listener; the 'li-' in the middle adds a sense of remoteness or grandeur. It is invariable (its form does not change for case) and here serves as the subject: 'That is the Day…'

2.meaning: the Day — a span of time; here the definite, decisive Day of Judgement and reckoning.
2.grammar: A noun with the article 'al-' (the). The final '-u' is the nominative ending; here it serves as the predicate identifying the subject 'that': 'That is the Day of Truth.' The definite article points to the one, specific Day already under discussion.
2.root: ي-و-م (y-w-m) — day, a period of time.

3.meaning: The truth, the reality, that which is firmly established and certain. Here it describes the Day of Judgement as the absolute, undeniable reality — what is real, just, and bound to happen, as opposed to falsehood (bāṭil).
3.grammar: A definite noun, 'the truth'. The final -u (nominative) marks it as the subject's complement here — it tells what 'That Day' IS ('That Day is the Truth'). The al- prefix ('the') makes it specific and absolute, not just 'a truth'.
3.root: ح-ق-ق (ḥ-q-q) — to be true, real, firmly established, rightfully due

4.meaning: 'So whoever' — a conjunction joining this to what came before, plus a conditional word meaning 'whoever, anyone who'. It opens a condition: 'so whoever does X, the result is Y'.
4.grammar: Two pieces joined: fa- ('so/then') links this sentence to the previous one as a consequence, and man is a conditional pronoun ('whoever') that sets up an if-then. Man itself does not change its ending. Here it governs two past-tense (perfect) verbs — shāʾa ('wills') and ittakhadha ('takes') — which keep their normal past form; the first states the condition and the second its answer.

5.meaning: He willed, he wished, he desired — the act of choosing or wanting something. In context: 'whoever wills (to do so)'.
5.grammar: A past-tense verb, 'he willed'. The final -a ending marks the doer as 'he' (one male, or anyone, matching the 'whoever' before it). Though past in form, after the conditional 'whoever' it carries the sense 'whoever should will'.
5.root: ش-ي-ء (sh-y-ʾ) — to will, to wish, to want

6.meaning: He took (for himself), he adopted, he chose and made (something his own). The form stresses taking deliberately for one's own benefit — here, taking a path/way back to one's Lord.
6.grammar: A past-tense verb in Form VIII (the pattern that adds reflexive force — 'take FOR ONESELF'). The final -a marks the doer as 'he' (matching 'whoever'). Functioning as the answer to the condition: 'whoever wills, takes…'. The doubled -tt- comes from the original t-prefix merging with the root's first letter.

7.meaning: 'To, towards, up to' — a preposition showing direction or the end-point of motion. Here it points to the goal: a way back 'to' one's Lord.
7.grammar: A preposition; it has no changeable ending of its own. It puts the word after it into the genitive case (here 'his Lord') and conveys movement or aiming toward a destination.

8.meaning: 'His Lord' — Rabb is one who owns, sustains, nurtures, and has full authority over what He cares for; far richer than 'master'. It combines ownership, upbringing, and care. With the ending 'his', it means each person's own Lord, Allah.
8.grammar: A noun, 'Lord', with 'his' attached at the end. The -i ending is genitive, required because the preposition 'to' (ilā) comes before it — 'TO his Lord'. The pronoun -hi ('his') refers back to the person ('whoever'); its vowel is -i to harmonize with the preceding -i sound.
8.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, sustain, master, bring up

9.meaning: A place of return / final resort — the destination one comes back to and settles in. For the transgressors, Hell is the home to which they ultimately return.
9.grammar: An indefinite noun of place ('ma-' pattern: the place where an action happens). The final -an marks indefiniteness and the accusative case — it is a second predicate/complement: Hell is, for them, 'a place of return.'

1.meaning: 'Indeed We' — a particle of strong emphasis (inna, 'truly/indeed') fused with the attached pronoun 'We'. Inna has no single English word; it firmly asserts and confirms the statement, removing any doubt. The 'We' is the royal/majestic 'We' of Allah.
1.grammar: The emphasis particle inna ('indeed') with 'We' attached as its subject. Inna strengthens and certifies the whole sentence ('We most certainly have warned…'). The attached -ā means 'We' (the majestic plural for Allah). The long vowel is simply stretched before the following hamza.
1.root: — (emphasis particle + attached pronoun; no triliteral root)

2.meaning: 'We have warned you' — to warn, to caution someone of a coming danger or punishment so they may take heed. The form is fully complete: We + warned + you (plural).
2.grammar: A past-tense Form IV verb (the pattern that makes it transitive/causative — 'to make aware, to warn'). The -nā ending means 'we' did it (the majestic 'We' of Allah); the attached -kum means 'you all' are the ones warned. So: 'We warned you-all'.
2.root: ن-ذ-ر (n-dh-r) — to warn, caution, give notice of danger

3.meaning: A punishment, torment, or chastisement — painful suffering imposed as a penalty. Here, the punishment of the Day of Judgement.
3.grammar: An indefinite noun, 'a punishment'. The -an ending (accusative with tanwīn) marks it as the direct object — the thing being warned about ('We warned you OF a punishment'). The -n sound (nunation) shows it is indefinite ('a' punishment, not 'the').
3.root: ع-ذ-ب (ʿ-dh-b) — to punish, torment, chastise

4.meaning: Near, close at hand — close in time, meaning soon/imminent. It describes the punishment as drawing near.
4.grammar: An adjective, 'near', describing the punishment. Its -an ending (accusative, indefinite) copies the ending of 'a punishment' (ʿadhāban) so the two agree — Arabic adjectives match their noun in case and definiteness. Together: 'a near punishment' / 'a punishment close at hand'.
4.root: ق-ر-ب (q-r-b) — to be near, close, to draw near

5.meaning: The Day — a specific day; here the Day of Resurrection, presented as the appointed moment on which the events that follow take place.
5.grammar: A noun ending in '-a' (accusative). The '-a' here functions adverbially — 'on the Day…' — anchoring the following clause in time (it stands as an adverb of time / or in apposition to the preceding 'appointed time'). The bare '-a' without tanwīn reflects that it is bound to the clause that follows it ('the Day [on which]…').
5.root: ي-و-م (y-w-m) — day, a span of time

6.meaning: He looks, gazes, sees, observes — and by extension considers or beholds. Here: each person 'will look upon / see' what their own hands have sent ahead.
6.grammar: A present/future-tense verb, 'he looks / will look'. The ya- prefix means the doer is 'he' (here 'the man / every person'). The final -u ending marks the plain present indicative — an ongoing or future fact ('looks / will look'), not a command.
6.root: ن-ظ-ر (n-ẓ-r) — to look, gaze, observe, consider

7.meaning: The man, the person, the human individual — a single human being. Used here generally for 'every person' who will face the reckoning.
7.grammar: A definite noun, 'the person', with al- ('the'). The -u ending is nominative, marking it as the subject — the one doing the looking ('the person looks / will look'). Though singular, it is meant generally: each and every individual.
7.root: م-ر-أ (m-r-ʾ) — manliness; a human being, a person

8.meaning: A relative/connector word meaning 'what' or 'that which' — here it points to the deeds and actions a person sent ahead. It introduces a clause: 'what (his hands) have put forward'.
8.grammar: This is an indeclinable particle/relative noun, so it has no case ending that changes — it simply stays 'mā'. It functions as a relative pronoun ('that which') heading the clause that follows; the verb after it tells us what was put forward.

9.meaning: To put forward, send ahead, or advance something — here it means the deeds a person has already done and dispatched ahead of themselves to meet them on the Day of Judgement.
9.grammar: A past-tense verb in the intensive (Form II) pattern, which adds force: not just 'to come before' but 'to actively send forward'. The final '-at' (a quiescent tā') is the feminine ending agreeing with the grammatically feminine subject that follows, 'his hands' — so it reads 'his hands have sent forward'.

10.meaning: His two hands — the dual of 'hand', here standing for the deeds and actions a person performs and is responsible for.
10.grammar: This is a dual noun ('two hands') acting as the subject of the verb, so it is in the nominative (doer) state. The dual subject ending normally appears as '-āni', but because the possessive '-hu' ('his') is attached, the final 'n' drops away, leaving 'yadā' + 'hu'. The '-hu' ending means 'his', telling us whose hands they are.

11.meaning: And he says / and he will say — introducing the disbeliever's despairing speech on that Day.
11.grammar: Begins with 'wa' ('and'), joining this to what came before. The verb is present/future tense: the 'ya-' prefix marks a third-person masculine singular subject ('he'), and the final '-u' is the indicative ending, which signals a plain, ongoing or future statement of fact ('he says / he will say'). The subject is 'the disbeliever', named next.

12.meaning: The disbeliever — one who rejects faith and conceals or denies the truth. The root sense is 'to cover up', so a kāfir is someone who covers over the truth and is ungrateful for Allah's signs.
12.grammar: The prefix 'al-' is the definite article 'the'. The word itself is an active participle ('one who disbelieves'). The final '-u' is the nominative ending, marking this as the subject — the one doing the saying in the previous verb ('and the disbeliever says').
12.root: ك-ف-ر (k-f-r) — to cover, conceal; hence to disbelieve, be ungrateful

13.meaning: An anguished cry of longing: 'O, if only I…!' It combines a call of distress with a wish for something now impossible — the disbeliever wishing they could undo their fate.
13.grammar: Opens with 'yā', normally a call ('O!') but here used to intensify the lament. 'Layta' is a particle expressing a wish for something contrary to reality ('if only…, would that…'). The attached '-nī' is the object pronoun 'me/I', the one being wished about. Layta makes its noun the accusative object, which is why the pronoun is the object-form '-nī': literally 'would that I…'.

14.meaning: 'I was / I had been' — from the verb 'to be'. Here it sets up the wish: 'that I had been (dust)', describing a state the speaker longs to have been in.
14.grammar: A past-tense form of the verb 'to be'. The ending '-tu' is the first-person singular marker, 'I' — 'I was / I had been'. As a verb of being, it expects a following word describing the state, given here in the accusative ('dust'). Paired with 'layta' before it, the sense is 'if only I had been…'.
14.root: ك-و-ن (k-w-n) — to be, to exist, come to be

15.meaning: Dust, dirt, the soil of the earth — what the body returns to. The disbeliever wishes to be mere lifeless dust rather than face the reckoning.
15.grammar: A noun, 'dust'. The final '-an' (written with tanwīn, the doubled fatḥa) is the indefinite accusative ending. It is accusative because it completes the verb 'I had been' — it is the thing the speaker wishes to have been ('that I had been dust'). The tanwīn ('-an') also signals that it is indefinite: 'dust' in general, not 'the dust'.
